name: Makkah
line: The valley of the Kaaba, birthplace of the Prophet ﷺ and the direction of every Muslim prayer.
story: Ibrahim left Hajar and baby Ismail in this barren valley, and father and son later raised the Kaaba. The tribe of Jurhum settled by Zamzam, and Quraysh came to rule it. Muhammad ﷺ was born here, received the Quran in its hills, was driven out, and returned in 630 to clear the idols.
note: The Quran also calls it Bakkah (3:96). Some scholars say Bakkah is the valley of the House itself and Makkah the wider town; others say they are two names for one place.

name: The Kaaba
line: The cube-shaped House of Allah, raised by Ibrahim and Ismail, the qiblah of Muslims everywhere.
story: Ibrahim and Ismail raised its foundations and prayed for a messenger from their offspring (2:127-129). Over the centuries it filled with idols; Quraysh rebuilt it when Muhammad ﷺ was 35, and he set the Black Stone in place. He cleansed it in 630, and it has been rebuilt since by Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hajjaj and the Ottoman sultan Murad IV.
note: Some reports say Adam or the angels first built it; the Quran speaks of Ibrahim and Ismail raising its foundations.

name: al-Masjid al-Haram
line: The Sacred Mosque around the Kaaba, the first mosque set on earth.
story: The open sanctuary around the Kaaba, where the Night Journey began (17:1). In the Prophet's ﷺ time it was a small yard ringed by houses; from Umar onward the caliphs bought land to widen it. The Ottomans built its domed arcades, and modern expansions hold millions of worshippers.

name: Zamzam
line: The well that burst out for Hajar and baby Ismail, still flowing beside the Kaaba.
story: When Hajar ran seven times between Safa and Marwah looking for water, an angel struck the ground and water gushed out beside Ismail. The well drew the tribe of Jurhum to settle, was later buried and forgotten, and was dug out again by Abd al-Muttalib after a dream. Pilgrims drink from it to this day.
note: Ibn Majah 3062 ('The water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for') is graded hasan or sahih by many scholars and weak by some. Abd al-Muttalib's re-digging is from the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq.

name: Safa and Marwah
line: Two low hills by the Kaaba where Hajar ran for water and pilgrims still walk.
story: Hajar ran between these hills searching for water for Ismail. The Quran names them among the symbols of Allah (2:158), and pilgrims walk between them seven times. From Safa the Prophet ﷺ first called Quraysh openly to Islam. Today the course lies inside the mosque.

name: Mina
line: The tent valley east of Makkah where pilgrims stone the pillars and offer sacrifice.
story: Tradition places Ibrahim's sacrifice here, and the stoning of Shaytan who tried to turn him back. Pilgrims camp here in the days of Hajj, stoning the pillars and sacrificing. At al-Aqabah, at the valley's edge, men of Yathrib pledged in 621 and 622 to protect the Prophet ﷺ.
note: The Quran does not name the place of the sacrifice (37:102-107); Mina is the tradition. Most scholars hold the son was Ismail; some early scholars said Ishaq.

name: Muzdalifah
line: The open plain between Arafat and Mina where pilgrims spend the night under the sky.
story: Pilgrims come here after sunset on the Day of Arafah. The Quran commands remembering Allah 'at al-Mash'ar al-Haram' (2:198), and in his Farewell Hajj the Prophet ﷺ prayed Maghrib and Isha here together and rested until dawn. Pilgrims gather their pebbles for the stoning here.

name: Arafat
line: The plain below the Mount of Mercy where standing on 9 Dhul-Hijjah is the heart of Hajj.
story: A wide plain about 20 km east of Makkah. 'Hajj is Arafah,' the Prophet ﷺ said. Here he gave his Farewell Sermon in 632, and here the verse 'This day I have perfected for you your religion' (5:3) was revealed, as Umar later confirmed.
note: A popular tradition says Adam and Hawwa met again at Arafat after the descent; it is not established in authentic hadith.

name: Cave of Hira
line: A small cave on the Mountain of Light where the first words of the Quran came down.
story: A narrow cave near the top of Jabal al-Nur, a few kilometres from the Kaaba. Before prophethood, Muhammad ﷺ used to retreat here for nights of worship. In 610 Jibril came to him here with the first revelation: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created' (96:1).
note: The verses cited were revealed here; the Quran does not name the cave.

name: Cave of Thawr
line: The mountain cave where the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid at the start of the Hijrah.
story: A cave on Mount Thawr, south of Makkah, where the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid for three nights while Quraysh hunted them. The trackers came right to its mouth. The Quran recalls the Prophet's ﷺ words to his frightened friend: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40).

name: Ta'if
line: A cool mountain town that stoned the Prophet ﷺ in 619 and embraced Islam a decade later.
story: Home of the Thaqif tribe, famous for grapes and the idol al-Lat. In 619 the Prophet ﷺ came seeking help and was driven out with stones; he refused to have them punished, hoping their children would worship Allah. After a siege in 630, Thaqif sent a delegation to Madinah and accepted Islam.
note: Most commentators say 'the two cities' of 43:31 are Makkah and Ta'if. The Christian slave Addas from Nineveh met the Prophet ﷺ in a garden here (Sirah of Ibn Ishaq).

name: Wadi Nakhla
line: The valley between Makkah and Ta'if where a band of jinn heard the Quran and believed.
story: As the Prophet ﷺ prayed at dawn in this valley, a group of jinn passed, listened to the Quran and went back to their people as warners (46:29-31). Surah al-Jinn begins with their words: 'Indeed, we have heard an amazing Qur'an' (72:1). Commentators link the night to the journey back from Ta'if.
note: The listening of the jinn is reported by Bukhari and Muslim. Whether it happened on the return from Ta'if is the view of many commentators, not certain. Coordinates are approximate.

name: al-Hudaybiyyah
line: A plain at the edge of the Haram where a truce that looked like a loss became 'a clear victory'.
story: In 628 Quraysh blocked about 1,400 Muslim pilgrims here. The Companions pledged under a tree to stand firm, and Allah was pleased with them (48:18). The Prophet ﷺ then signed a ten-year truce whose terms seemed harsh, but the Quran called it 'a clear victory' (48:1), and within two years Makkah opened.
note: The site is generally identified with al-Shumaysi on the old Jeddah road.

name: Hunayn
line: The valley where a proud Muslim army broke, then rallied around the Prophet ﷺ.
story: Weeks after the conquest of Makkah in 630, the Hawazin ambushed a Muslim army of about 12,000 in this valley on the road to Ta'if, and many fled. The Prophet ﷺ stood firm calling out, the Companions rallied, and victory came. The Quran warns that their great numbers 'did not avail you at all' (9:25).
note: The exact battlefield is not certain; coordinates are approximate.

name: Jeddah
line: Makkah's sea gate, where most pilgrims have arrived by ship for nearly fourteen centuries.
story: A fishing settlement on the Red Sea that the caliph Uthman chose as Makkah's port in 647. For centuries pilgrims from Africa, India and the Malay world landed here. A popular tradition placed the tomb of Hawwa, mother of humankind, in its old cemetery.
note: The tomb of Hawwa is a popular tradition with no sound basis.

name: Madinah
line: The oasis that welcomed the Prophet ﷺ and became the first home of the Muslim community.
story: An oasis called Yathrib, home of the Aws, the Khazraj and Jewish tribes. In 622 its people welcomed the Prophet ﷺ, and it became the first Muslim community and the capital of the first caliphs. The Prophet ﷺ is buried here, and he said faith will return to Madinah as a snake returns to its hole.

name: al-Masjid al-Nabawi
line: The Prophet's ﷺ Mosque in Madinah, where he lived, taught and is buried.
story: Built by the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions in 622 of mud brick and palm trunks, it was mosque, school, court and shelter for the poor of the Suffah. His grave, with those of Abu Bakr and Umar, lies inside beneath the Green Dome. He said the space between his house and his pulpit is a garden of Paradise.
note: Scholars differ whether 9:108, 'a mosque founded on righteousness from the first day', means Quba or this mosque; a narration in Sahih Muslim points to this one.

name: Quba Mosque
line: The first mosque of Islam, built on the edge of Madinah on the day of the Hijrah.
story: When the Prophet ﷺ reached Quba on the Hijrah in 622, he stayed some days and laid the first mosque in Islam. He kept visiting it every Saturday, walking or riding. Many scholars say it is the mosque 'founded on righteousness from the first day' (9:108).
note: 9:107 refers to the 'mosque of harm' built nearby by hypocrites; the Prophet ﷺ had it pulled down after Tabuk.

name: Masjid al-Qiblatayn
line: The 'mosque of the two qiblahs', where tradition says the prayer turned from Jerusalem to Makkah.
story: For about sixteen months in Madinah the Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem. In 624 the command came to turn toward the Sacred Mosque (2:144). Tradition says the change came during a prayer in this mosque of the Banu Salimah, and the worshippers turned around mid-prayer.
note: Bukhari reports a similar turning at Quba during Fajr; which mosque came first is debated.

name: Jannat al-Baqi
line: The old cemetery of Madinah, resting place of thousands of Companions and the Prophet's ﷺ family.
story: Here lie the Prophet's ﷺ son Ibrahim, his daughters, many of his wives, the caliph Uthman, al-Hasan, and thousands of Companions; most scholars say Fatimah too. The Prophet ﷺ used to go out at night to greet its dead and pray for them.
note: Fatimah's grave is placed here by most reports; its exact spot is unknown.

name: Mount Uhud
line: The red mountain north of Madinah where the Muslims learned a hard lesson in obedience.
story: In 625 Quraysh came to avenge Badr. When the archers left their post on a hill to gather spoils, Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry struck from behind; about seventy Muslims were martyred, among them Hamzah, buried at the mountain's foot. Yet the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Uhud is a mountain that loves us, and we love it.'
note: 'Uhud is a mountain that loves us' is reported by Bukhari and Muslim.

name: Badr
line: The wells where 313 believers met an army three times their size: the Day of the Criterion.
story: Badr was a watering place on the caravan road southwest of Madinah. In Ramadan 624 the Muslims faced a Makkan army of about a thousand and won; Abu Jahl was killed. The Quran calls it 'the day of criterion, the day when the two armies met' (8:41), and the people of Badr hold a rank of their own.

name: Khaybar
line: A fortified oasis north of Madinah, opened in 628 under the banner given to Ali.
story: An oasis of forts and palm groves held by Jewish tribes, some of whom had been exiled from Madinah. In 628 the Muslims took its forts one by one; the Prophet ﷺ gave the banner to 'a man who loves Allah and His Messenger', and it was Ali. The people stayed to farm the land for half the harvest.
note: The banner hadith is reported by Bukhari and Muslim. Commentators say the spoils promised in 48:18-20 include Khaybar.

name: Tabuk
line: The northern oasis where the Prophet ﷺ led his last expedition in the 'hour of hardship'.
story: In the burning summer of 630, the Prophet ﷺ led about 30,000 men here to meet a Byzantine threat that never came. The Quran calls it 'the hour of difficulty' (9:117), a test that exposed the hypocrites. Three sincere men who stayed behind, among them Ka'b ibn Malik, were forgiven after fifty days of boycott (9:118).

name: Mu'tah
line: The village in Jordan where three commanders fell in turn and Khalid became the Sword of Allah.
story: In 629 a Muslim force of 3,000 met a far larger Byzantine and Arab army here, east of the Dead Sea. Zayd ibn Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and Abdullah ibn Rawahah each took the banner and were martyred. Khalid ibn al-Walid led the rest safely home, and the Prophet ﷺ called him one of the swords of Allah.
note: The account of the three commanders and Khalid is reported by Bukhari.

name: Najran
line: A valley town of south Arabia, home of early Arab Christians and linked to the People of the Ditch.
story: An old centre of Arabian Christianity. Tradition links it to the People of the Ditch, believers burned alive by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas around 523 (85:4-8). In 631 its Christian delegation debated the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah, declined the mutual curse (3:61), and made a treaty with him.
note: Most commentators place the Ditch (85:4) at Najran; the Quran does not name the place.

name: Dumat al-Jandal
line: A desert fortress town at the head of Wadi Sirhan, gateway between Arabia and Syria.
story: An ancient oasis with a stone citadel, a meeting point of Arabia, Iraq and Syria. The Prophet ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid from Tabuk to its ruler Ukaydir in 630, and the town came to terms. Its old mosque is named after Umar.

name: Jerusalem
line: City of Dawud and Sulayman, first qiblah of Islam and goal of the Night Journey.
story: Dawud made it his capital and Sulayman built the house of worship. Rome razed it and renamed it Aelia; in 637 Umar travelled from Madinah to receive its keys and guaranteed its people their churches and lives. Crusaders took it in 1099 with great slaughter, and Salah al-Din restored it to Muslim rule in 1187 without revenge.
note: Many commentators say the ruined town of 2:259 is Jerusalem after Bukhtanassar's attack; others name other towns.

name: al-Masjid al-Aqsa
line: The Farthest Mosque, second house of worship on earth and third holiest place in Islam.
story: The Prophet ﷺ said it was set on earth forty years after the Sacred Mosque. On the Night Journey he led the prophets in prayer here before rising through the heavens. Umar cleared the site in 637; Abd al-Malik raised the Dome of the Rock in 691, and the congregational mosque followed under al-Walid.
note: In early usage al-Masjid al-Aqsa means the whole walled sanctuary, not only the mosque building.

name: al-Sham
line: The Levant, which the Quran calls 'the land which We had blessed for the worlds'.
story: The lands of today's Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. Ibrahim and Lut were delivered here (21:71), and it was home to Ishaq, Yaqub, Dawud, Sulayman, Zakariya and Isa. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for its blessing, and it became the heart of the Umayyad caliphate.
note: Commentators identify 'the land We blessed' with al-Sham, most centring it on Jerusalem.

name: Canaan
line: The land between the Jordan and the sea where Ibrahim settled and Yaqub raised his sons.
story: Ibrahim came here from Iraq with Sarah and Lut, and Ishaq and Yaqub lived here as herdsmen. From here Yusuf's brothers took him to the well, and later Yaqub's whole family went down to Egypt (12:99-100). Commentators say the 'Holy Land' Musa told his people to enter (5:21) is this land.

name: Hebron (al-Khalil)
line: The hill town named after Ibrahim, Friend of Allah, where tradition places his tomb.
story: The town takes its Arabic name from Ibrahim, Khalil Allah. Here, tradition says, the angels came to him as guests with news of Ishaq (11:69-73). Ibrahim, Sarah, Ishaq, Yaqub and their wives are held to rest in the cave beneath the Ibrahimi Mosque, whose great walls go back to Herod.
note: The burial tradition is shared with Jews and Christians; the Quran does not name the place.

name: Sodom and the Dead Sea
line: The salt sea Arabs call Bahr Lut, beside which the towns of Lut's people were overturned.
story: Lut's towns were turned upside down and rained with stones of baked clay (11:82). The Arabs still call this sea, the lowest place on earth, Bahr Lut, the Sea of Lut. The Quran told Quraysh, who passed this way on their trade journeys, that they pass by the ruins morning and night (37:137-138).
note: The exact site of Sodom is unknown; candidates lie at both ends of the Dead Sea.

name: Jericho (Ariha)
line: One of the oldest towns on earth, an oasis by the Jordan just north of the Dead Sea.
story: Many commentators say Jericho was 'the town' Bani Israil were told to enter humbly, saying 'Hittah', 'relieve us of our burdens' (2:58), and that Yusha' took it after the forty years of wandering. Some of them changed the word they were told to say and were punished (2:59).
note: Commentators differ: some say the town of 2:58 was Jerusalem, others Jericho.

name: Valley of Elah
line: The valley where tradition sets the duel in which young Dawud killed Jalut.
story: Talut's small army, tested at a river, faced Jalut's forces. 'How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah,' said the faithful (2:249). Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him kingship and prophethood (2:251). Biblical tradition places the battle in this valley southwest of Jerusalem.
note: The Quran does not name the battlefield; the location is from biblical tradition.

name: Bethlehem
line: The town south of Jerusalem where Christian tradition places the birth of Isa.
story: The Quran tells how Maryam withdrew 'to a remote place' and gave birth under a palm tree, which gave her fresh dates, while a stream ran below her (19:22-26). Christians have long placed the birth in Bethlehem, where the Church of the Nativity, begun under Constantine, still stands.
note: The Quran does not name the place. Some commentators placed the 'high ground with flowing water' (23:50) at Bethlehem or Jerusalem; others at Damascus or Egypt.

name: Nazareth
line: The Galilee town where Isa grew up, and perhaps the root of the Quran's word for Christians.
story: Maryam lived here and Isa grew up here. The Quran calls Christians 'Nasara' (5:14), which many scholars link to Nazareth (al-Nasirah). Others connect the word to 'ansar', the helpers of Allah, as the disciples called themselves (61:14).
note: Both derivations of Nasara are given by the commentators.

name: Galilee and Tiberias
line: The green hill country around the Lake of Tiberias where Isa preached and called his disciples.
story: Isa healed, preached and called the Hawariyyun here (3:52), and here Christian tradition sets many of his miracles. Tiberias on the lake became a Muslim town in 634. In the hadith of the end times, Yajuj and Majuj pass by the lake and drink it dry.

name: Hawran and Busra
line: A black-stone plain in southern Syria tied by tradition to Ayyub and by the Sirah to the monk Bahira.
story: Tradition places the long trial of Ayyub here, at Shaykh Sa'd near Nawa, where a rock and a spring bear his name (38:41-44). Its chief town, Busra, was a Roman caravan city. The young Muhammad ﷺ is said to have met the monk Bahira there on a trade journey with Abu Talib.
note: The Quran does not name Ayyub's land; other traditions place him in Urfa or Oman. Tirmidhi 3620 (Bahira) is graded hasan by Tirmidhi; some critics question parts of it.

name: Baalbek
line: A temple city in Lebanon whose name carries the god Ba'l that Ilyas preached against.
story: Ilyas asked his people: 'Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators?' (37:125). Many commentators link his mission to this city of the Bekaa valley, whose name joins Ba'l. Its giant Roman temples, later a fortress, amazed the Muslim geographers.
note: The link to Ilyas comes from the name; the Quran does not name his city.

name: Antioch
line: The old Syrian capital that tradition makes 'the town' of Surah Ya-Sin.
story: Surah Ya-Sin tells of a town that rejected messengers until a man came running from the far end of the city to defend them, and was killed (36:13-27). Many commentators said the town was Antioch and named the man Habib al-Najjar; a mosque in his name stands there. Antioch was later a Crusader principality.
note: The town and the man's name come from the commentators, not the Quran.

name: Damascus
line: One of the oldest living cities, capital of the Umayyads and, in the hadith, where Isa will descend.
story: Damascus surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubaydah in 634. As the Umayyad capital it ruled from Spain to Sindh, and al-Walid built its Great Mosque in 705. Nur al-Din and Salah al-Din ruled from here, and the Prophet ﷺ said Isa will descend by a white minaret east of Damascus.
note: A few commentators identified Iram (89:7) or the 'high ground' of 23:50 with Damascus; most did not.

name: Aleppo
line: A great citadel city of northern Syria, seat of Sayf al-Dawla and Nur al-Din.
story: Taken by the Muslims in 637, it flourished under the Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla, whose court in the 900s gathered the poet al-Mutanabbi and the philosopher al-Farabi. Nur al-Din made it a base against the Crusaders, and its citadel withstood many sieges before the Mongols sacked it in 1260.

name: Urfa (Edessa)
line: The city where local tradition says Namrud threw Ibrahim into the fire.
story: Muslim, Jewish and Christian traditions here hold that Ibrahim was born in a cave in Urfa and thrown into a fire that Allah made 'coolness and safety' (21:69). The pools of sacred fish mark the spot. As Edessa it became the first Crusader state in 1098, and Zengi's capture of it in 1144 launched the Second Crusade.
note: The Quran does not name the place of the fire; Ur, Kutha (Iraq) and Urfa are all claimed.

name: Harran
line: An ancient city of star-worshippers on Ibrahim's road from Iraq to Canaan.
story: Tradition says Ibrahim lived in Harran before leaving for Canaan, among a people who worshipped the moon and stars (6:76-78). Its star-worshipping Sabians survived into Abbasid times and gave Baghdad scholars such as the mathematician Thabit ibn Qurra. The last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, ruled from here.
note: Whether the Sabians of Harran are the Sabi'un of the Quran (2:62) is debated.

name: Mesopotamia
line: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates, where cities, writing and kingship began.
story: Many commentators place the people of Nuh in this land, and most say Ibrahim was born here. It later held Babylon, Nineveh and Ctesiphon, and after Islam came, Kufa, Basra and Baghdad.
note: The Quran does not say where Nuh lived; Iraq is the most common view among historians and commentators.

name: Uruk
line: Perhaps the world's first true city, where writing on clay began.
story: Around 3500 to 3100 BCE Uruk grew into a city of tens of thousands, with great temples and the earliest writing. It shows the world into which the early messengers came: kings, temples and many gods.

name: Ur
line: The Sumerian moon-god city that many historians make Ibrahim's birthplace.
story: A great city near the Euphrates with a towering ziggurat to the moon god. Jewish and Christian tradition, followed by many Muslim historians, makes it the place where Ibrahim reasoned with his people about the star, the moon and the sun (6:76-79) and broke their idols (21:57-58).
note: The Quran does not name Ibrahim's city; Ur, Kutha and Urfa are all suggested.

name: Akkad
line: Lost capital of Sargon, who built the first known empire around 2300 BCE.
story: Sargon of Akkad united the cities of Mesopotamia into the first known empire. Its language, Akkadian, is the oldest written Semitic tongue, a distant relative of Arabic. The city's site has never been found.
note: Coordinates are a guess; the site is unknown.

name: Babylon (Babil)
line: The great city on the Euphrates that the Quran names in the story of Harut and Marut.
story: Babil is named in the Quran as the place where two angels, Harut and Marut, taught a trial to the people (2:102). Many commentators set Ibrahim's clash with Namrud in this land. Nebuchadnezzar carried Bani Israil captive here, and Cyrus of Persia took it in 539 BCE.
note: Linking Namrud to Babylon is tradition, not Quran. Whether Harut and Marut were angels or men is debated.

name: Nineveh
line: The Assyrian capital on the Tigris, traditionally the city of Yunus.
story: Tradition says Yunus was sent to Nineveh, opposite today's Mosul. His people alone among the nations believed before the punishment fell and were spared (10:98). Here too in 627 Heraclius crushed the Persian army, as the Quran had foretold Rome's victory (30:2-4).
note: The Quran does not name Yunus's city; Nineveh is the tradition. At Ta'if, the slave Addas of Nineveh recognised the Prophet ﷺ as Yunus's brother (Sirah of Ibn Ishaq).

name: Mosul
line: The city facing Nineveh across the Tigris, base of Zengi and Nur al-Din.
story: Founded as a Muslim garrison opposite ruined Nineveh in the 640s. In the 1100s Imad al-Din Zengi ruled from here and began the fight back against the Crusaders, carried on by his son Nur al-Din. Its leaning al-Hadba minaret, built by Nur al-Din, became the city's symbol.

name: Ctesiphon (al-Mada'in)
line: The Persian capital whose king tore up the Prophet's ﷺ letter, and whose palace still stands.
story: Twin-city capital of the Parthian and Sasanian kings on the Tigris; its great brick arch, the Taq Kisra, still stands. Khosrow II tore up the Prophet's ﷺ letter here. In 637 Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas entered it, and Salman al-Farisi later governed it and is buried nearby.

name: al-Hirah
line: Capital of the Arab Lakhmid kings, an early home of Arabic writing.
story: The Lakhmids ruled the desert Arabs from here as allies of Persia, and many of its people were Christians. Arab tradition says the Arabic script spread to Makkah from al-Hirah and al-Anbar. Khalid ibn al-Walid took it in 633, and Kufa was later founded nearby.
note: The origin of the Arabic script is debated; most scholars now trace it to Nabataean writing.

name: al-Qadisiyyah
line: The desert battlefield where the Muslims broke Sasanian Persia.
story: On the edge of the Iraqi desert, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the Sasanian army over several days, probably in 636; its commander Rustam was killed. Within a year the Persian capital Ctesiphon fell, opening Iraq to Islam.
note: The year is given as 636 or 637 in different sources.

name: Kufa
line: A garrison city that became Ali's capital and a great school of Quran, grammar and fiqh.
story: Founded by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas around 638. Ali made it his capital and was struck down in its mosque in 661. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud taught the Quran here, Abu Hanifah grew up and taught here, and the first Abbasid caliph was proclaimed here in 749.

name: Najaf
line: The town beside Kufa that grew around the shrine tradition holds to be Ali's tomb.
story: Ali was buried secretly after his death in 661 to protect his grave. In Abbasid times a tomb near Kufa became widely accepted as his, and the town of Najaf grew around it. It became a great centre of Shi'i learning.
note: Early reports differ on where Ali was buried; Najaf is the dominant tradition.

name: Basra
line: A port at the head of the Gulf that became a city of scholars, grammarians and seafarers.
story: Founded as a garrison under Umar around 636. Al-Hasan al-Basri preached here, al-Khalil and his student Sibawayh shaped Arabic grammar, and Rabi'a al-Adawiyya taught pure love of Allah. Its ships sailed to India and China, the world of the Sindbad tales.

name: Karbala
line: The plain by the Euphrates where al-Husayn, the Prophet's ﷺ grandson, was killed in 680.
story: On 10 Muharram 680 an Umayyad army surrounded al-Husayn ibn Ali, his family and companions here and killed him with most of the men. His sister Zaynab spoke for the survivors. His shrine grew into a city, and for all Muslims the day stands for courage against injustice.

name: Baghdad
line: The Round City of Peace, capital of the Abbasids and home of the House of Wisdom.
story: The caliph al-Mansur founded it in 762 as a round 'City of Peace' on the Tigris. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun it was among the largest cities on earth, where Greek, Persian and Indian learning was translated into Arabic. The Mongols sacked it in 1258 and killed the last Abbasid caliph there.

name: Samarra
line: The Abbasid capital of the 800s, famous for its spiral minaret.
story: The caliph al-Mu'tasim built Samarra in 836 as a new capital away from crowded Baghdad. For half a century it spread for miles along the Tigris; its Great Mosque, finished in 852 with the spiral Malwiya minaret, was then the largest in the world. The caliphs went back to Baghdad in 892.

name: Darb Zubaydah
line: The pilgrim road from Kufa to Makkah, lined with wells paid for by a queen.
story: A road of about 1,400 km across Arabia with wells, cisterns and rest stations every day's march. It is named after Zubaydah, wife of Harun al-Rashid, who funded much of its water works, as well as a channel bringing spring water to Makkah and Arafat.

name: Egypt (Misr)
line: The Nile land where Yusuf rose to power and Musa faced Firaun, named in the Quran as Misr.
story: Yusuf rose here from slave to keeper of the storehouses, and Musa confronted Firaun here. Hajar, mother of Ismail, came from Egypt, as did Mariya, mother of the Prophet's ﷺ son Ibrahim. Amr ibn al-As opened it in 641, and it became the seat of the Fatimids, Ayyubids and Mamluks.
note: Some commentators read 'misr' in 2:61 as 'a town', not Egypt.

name: The Nile (al-Yamm)
line: The river that carried baby Musa in a chest to Firaun's own palace.
story: Musa's mother was inspired to cast him into 'al-yamm', and the river laid him on the bank of his enemy (20:39). Firaun boasted of 'these rivers flowing beneath me' (43:51). Amr ibn al-As founded Fustat on its bank, and Cairo grew beside it.
note: 'Al-yamm' can mean sea or river; here the commentators say the Nile.

name: Memphis
line: The first capital of united Egypt, near the pyramids.
story: Founded around 3100 BCE where the Nile valley meets the delta, it was capital of the pyramid builders. Some Muslim historians placed Yusuf's prison and palace at Memphis, which Arab writers called Manf; the ruler of Yusuf's time is called 'the king', not Pharaoh, in the Quran (12:43).
note: Yusuf's city is not named in the Quran or known to historians.

name: Giza
line: Plateau of the Great Pyramid, the tallest building on earth for nearly 4,000 years.
story: The Great Pyramid of Khufu was raised around 2560 BCE. The Muslim physician Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi studied and measured the pyramids around 1200. The Quran recalls Firaun 'of the stakes' (89:10) and his order to Haman to bake bricks for a tower (28:38).
note: The Quran does not mention the pyramids, which are far older than the Firaun of Musa; linking 'the stakes' to monuments is one interpretation among several.

name: Cairo and Fustat
line: Amr's tent-city on the Nile that became Cairo, 'the Victorious', city of al-Azhar.
story: Amr ibn al-As founded Fustat beside the Nile in 641; his mosque, rebuilt many times, still stands. In 969 the Fatimids built al-Qahira and al-Azhar beside it. Under Salah al-Din and the Mamluks, Cairo became the greatest city of the Muslim world and home of the Abbasid caliphs after 1258.

name: Alexandria
line: Alexander's city by the sea, the learned capital of Egypt for a thousand years.
story: Founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BCE, it was famous for its lighthouse and library under the Ptolemies and Romans. Its ruler, the Muqawqis, received the Prophet's ﷺ letter and sent gifts, among them Mariya. Amr ibn al-As took it in 641-642, and it remained Egypt's great Mediterranean port.
note: The Muqawqis is often identified with Cyrus, patriarch of Alexandria; this is debated.

name: Suez
line: The canal town joining the Mediterranean and Red Seas, opened in 1869.
story: Near the old port of al-Qulzum, the Suez Canal opened in 1869, cutting the voyage from Europe to India. It sped pilgrim steamships to Jeddah, but also drew Britain into occupying Egypt in 1882.

name: The Sea Crossing (Red Sea)
line: The sea that split for Musa and Bani Israil and closed over Firaun's army.
story: Musa struck the sea with his staff and it parted, each side 'like a great towering mountain' (26:63). Bani Israil crossed; Firaun followed and drowned, declaring belief only when it was too late (10:90). The Prophet ﷺ fasted on Ashura, 10 Muharram, the day of this rescue, and told Muslims to fast it.
note: The crossing point is unknown: suggestions include the Gulf of Suez, the Bitter Lakes and the Gulf of Aqaba.

name: Sinai (the Wilderness)
line: The wilderness where Bani Israil wandered forty years, fed with manna and quails.
story: After Bani Israil refused to enter the Holy Land, they wandered here for forty years (5:26). Allah shaded them with clouds and sent manna and quails (2:57), and Musa struck the rock so twelve springs flowed (2:60). Here, too, many commentators set the golden calf of al-Samiri.
note: The wandering's location is traditional, and where the cow story (2:67-73) happened is not stated.

name: Mount Sinai (al-Tur)
line: The mountain where Allah spoke to Musa and gave him the Torah; the Quran swears by it.
story: Here Allah spoke to Musa, gave him the tablets, and raised the mountain above Bani Israil as they took their covenant (2:63). The Quran swears by it twice (52:1, 95:2) and praises the olive tree that grows from it (23:20). Tradition places it at Jabal Musa, where St Catherine's monastery has stood since the 500s.
note: Jabal Musa is a later identification; other peaks in Sinai and northwest Arabia are proposed. A 'covenant of the Prophet ﷺ' kept at the monastery is of disputed authenticity.

name: Valley of Tuwa
line: The 'sacred valley of Tuwa' where Musa saw the fire and was called to prophethood.
story: Returning from Madyan with his family, Musa saw a fire on the mountainside and went to it. From a tree in the blessed valley, Allah called him: 'Remove your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa' (20:12). There he was given the staff and the shining hand and sent to Firaun.
note: Placed by tradition below Jabal Musa. A different Dhu Tuwa near Makkah is where the Prophet ﷺ camped before entering in 630.

name: Junction of the Two Seas
line: The meeting of the seas where Musa found Khidr, the servant given knowledge from Allah.
story: Musa set out with his young servant to reach 'the junction of the two seas' (18:60). There the fish they carried slipped into the water, and there they met Khidr, who taught Musa patience through three strange deeds. Where it lies is unknown.
note: Pin placed at Ras Muhammad, the tip of Sinai where the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba meet, one suggestion among several; others say Bab al-Mandab, or where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic.

name: Madyan
line: The land of Shuayb's people, where Musa found refuge, a wife and ten years of work.
story: On the east shore of the Gulf of Aqaba lived the people of Shuayb, who cheated in weights and measures and were destroyed by a terrible blast (11:94). Musa fled here from Egypt, watered the flocks of two sisters at a well, married one of them and served her father for ten years (28:22-28).
note: Most commentators say Musa's father-in-law was Shuayb; others say he was another righteous man. Whether the 'people of the Aykah' (26:176) were the same people is debated.

name: Ayla (Aqaba)
line: A port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, the 'town by the sea' of the Sabbath-breakers in tradition.
story: Many commentators say 'the town that stood by the sea', whose people broke the Sabbath to catch fish and were turned into apes, was Ayla (7:163-166). During the Tabuk expedition in 630 its Christian ruler came to the Prophet ﷺ and made a treaty. Ruins of an early Islamic town have been dug up in Aqaba.
note: The town of 7:163 is not named in the Quran; Ayla is the most common view.

name: al-Hijr (Hegra)
line: The rocky land of Thamud, who carved homes from mountains and killed Salih's she-camel.
story: Thamud carved houses from the mountains 'feeling secure' (15:82) and hamstrung the she-camel sent as a sign, so the blast seized them. The ornate tombs seen today were cut later by the Nabataeans. Passing here on the way to Tabuk, the Prophet ﷺ told the Companions to enter only weeping and not to use its water.
note: The visible tombs are Nabataean, from around the 1st century, centuries after Thamud; the Quran places Thamud in this region.

name: Iram of the Pillars
line: 'Iram, who had lofty pillars, the likes of whom had never been created in the land' (89:7-8).
story: Iram was the city or tribe of Ad, the people of Hud, proud of their strength and tall buildings, destroyed by a furious wind for seven nights and eight days (69:6-7). Its place is unknown. Some link it to the lost caravan town of Ubar in the Omani desert, others to Hadramawt.
note: Some scholars say Iram was a tribe, not a city. The pin is placed at Shisr in Oman, claimed in the 1990s to be Ubar; that claim is disputed.

name: al-Ahqaf
line: The 'curving sand dunes' of south Arabia where Hud warned the people of Ad.
story: 'Mention the brother of Ad, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf' (46:21). Ad saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and cried, 'This is a cloud bringing us rain!' It was a wind carrying painful punishment, and nothing was left but their dwellings (46:24-25). Tradition places the dunes on the edge of the Empty Quarter near Hadramawt.

name: Hadramawt
line: A deep valley of south Arabia, home of Hud's tomb in tradition and of Islam's seafaring scholars.
story: A shrine in Hadramawt is visited as the tomb of the prophet Hud. Its people joined Islam in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime. Centuries later, scholars and traders from Tarim and other towns of Hadramawt carried Islam across the Indian Ocean to East Africa, India and the Malay world.
note: The tomb of Hud is a tradition; its authenticity is unknown.

name: al-Rass
line: The mysterious 'people of the well', named twice among the destroyed nations.
story: The Quran lists the Ashab al-Rass between Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh (25:38, 50:12) but tells no story. Commentators differ widely: a people who threw their prophet into a well, a town in Najd, or a land by the Aras river in the Caucasus.
note: The pin is placed at the town of al-Rass in Qassim, which carries the name; the real site is unknown.

name: Saba and Ma'rib
line: Capital of the Queen of Sheba, whose great dam burst when her people turned ungrateful.
story: Saba grew rich from incense and a dam that watered 'two gardens, on the right and on the left' (34:15). The hoopoe brought Sulayman news of its queen, who came to him and submitted with him to Allah (27:44). When later generations turned away, the 'flood of the dam' scattered its tribes across Arabia (34:16).
note: The queen's name, Bilqis, comes from the commentators, not the Quran. The dam's last collapse is usually dated around 570 CE.

name: Sana'a
line: Yemen's highland capital, where Abraha built a church to rival the Kaaba.
story: An ancient city famed for the Ghumdan palace. The Aksumite governor Abraha built a great church here to draw Arab pilgrims away from Makkah, then marched on the Kaaba with an elephant (105:1-5). Its Great Mosque is said to date from the Prophet's ﷺ time; very early Quran pages were found hidden in its roof in 1972.
note: The church story is from the Sirah and early histories; the Quran names only the 'companions of the elephant'.

name: Aden
line: A harbour in an old volcano at the mouth of the Red Sea, named in a sign of the Hour.
story: For thousands of years ships between India, Africa and Egypt called here. Yemen entered Islam in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, and Britain held Aden from 1839 to 1967. Among the major signs of the Hour, the Prophet ﷺ named a fire that will come out of Yemen, from the depths of Aden, driving people to their gathering.

name: Muscat
line: Oman's port, base of a sea empire that drove out the Portuguese and ruled Zanzibar.
story: Oman accepted Islam by letter from the Prophet ﷺ, sent to its kings Jayfar and Abd. In 1650 the Omanis drove the Portuguese from Muscat and built a sea empire reaching Zanzibar and the Swahili coast.

name: Petra
line: The rose-red rock city of the Nabataean Arabs, near the traditional tomb of Harun.
story: Capital of the Nabataeans, carved into cliffs in southern Jordan and rich from the incense road. Rome annexed it in 106 CE. Its rock-cut tombs share the style of al-Hijr, which the Nabataeans also ruled. A shrine on nearby Jabal Harun is held by tradition to be the tomb of Harun.
note: Harun's tomb on Jabal Harun is tradition, not established.

name: Palmyra (Tadmur)
line: A caravan city of the Syrian desert whose queen Zenobia defied Rome.
story: Its queen Zenobia ruled from Egypt to Anatolia until Rome captured her in 272. Khalid ibn al-Walid passed it on his desert march to Syria in 634, and it came to terms. Arab poets credited its colossal ruins to the jinn who built for Sulayman.
note: The jinn story is Arab legend, not Quran; the Quran says only that jinn built for Sulayman (34:12-13).

name: Aksum (Abyssinia)
line: Capital of the Christian kingdom whose Najashi sheltered the first Muslim refugees.
story: Aksum was famed for its tall stone obelisks and trade with Rome and India. Its ruler, the Najashi, sheltered the first Muslim refugees in 615 and refused Quraysh's demand to hand them back after hearing Surah Maryam. When he died, the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer for him in Madinah.
note: Historians debate whether the Najashi's court was at Aksum itself. Many commentators link 5:83, Christians moved to tears by the Quran, to the Najashi and his people.

name: Harar
line: A walled Muslim city of eastern Ethiopia, full of mosques and shrines.
story: Harar grew as a centre of Islamic learning and trade in the Horn of Africa and was the base of the Adal sultanate. From here Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi conquered much of Ethiopia in the 1530s. Its city wall, the Jugol, dates from the 1500s, and some locals call it the fourth holy city of Islam.

name: Kairouan
line: The first Muslim city of the Maghrib, founded by Uqba ibn Nafi.
story: Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan in 670 as the base for the advance across North Africa. Its Great Mosque became the model for mosques across the Maghrib, and its scholars, led by Sahnun, spread the Maliki school through Africa and Spain. Under the Aghlabids it was the capital of Ifriqiya, from which Sicily was won.

name: Mahdia
line: A walled town on a narrow cape, first capital of the Fatimid caliphs.
story: The first Fatimid caliph, Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi, founded Mahdia in 916 as his capital, guarded by sea on three sides. From here the Fatimids took Egypt in 969 and moved their capital to Cairo.

name: Tunis
line: The city beside ruined Carthage, home of the Zaytuna mosque and birthplace of Ibn Khaldun.
story: Tunis grew beside the ruins of Carthage after the Muslims took the region around 698. Its Zaytuna mosque became one of the great schools of the Maghrib, and Ibn Khaldun was born here in 1332. It was the Hafsid capital, later an Ottoman province, and a French protectorate from 1881.

name: Tiaret
line: The old Rustamid capital, near the castle where Ibn Khaldun wrote his Muqaddimah.
story: Tahart was capital of the Rustamid state from 777 to 909. Nearby, at the castle of Qal'at Ibn Salama, Ibn Khaldun withdrew in 1375 and wrote the Muqaddimah, laying foundations for the study of history and society.

name: Algiers
line: An Ottoman sea-fortress on the Mediterranean, invaded by France in 1830.
story: The Barbarossa brothers made Algiers an Ottoman stronghold in the early 1500s. France invaded in 1830; Emir Abd al-Qadir, a scholar and Sufi, led resistance for fifteen years. Algeria won independence in 1962 after a bitter war.

name: Fez
line: A Moroccan city of scholars and craftsmen, home of al-Qarawiyyin, founded by a woman.
story: Founded by the Idrisids around 789 to 808. In 859 Fatimah al-Fihri, a woman from Kairouan, founded the mosque of al-Qarawiyyin, often called the oldest university still teaching. Under the Marinids, Fez was a capital of learning and craft.

name: Marrakesh
line: The red city of the Almoravids and Almohads, which gave Morocco its name.
story: Founded around 1070 by the Almoravids as the capital of an empire from Senegal to Spain. The Almohads built its Kutubiyya mosque, whose minaret was a model for the Giralda of Seville. Europeans named the whole country, Morocco, after it.

name: Rabat
line: Named after a frontier fort of warrior-ascetics; Morocco's capital today.
story: Its name comes from 'ribat', a fortified post for men who guarded the frontier and worshipped. The Almohad caliph Ya'qub al-Mansur planned a vast mosque here in the 1190s; its unfinished Hassan Tower still stands. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation was founded here in 1969.

name: Tangier
line: The port on the Strait where Tariq set out for Spain and Ibn Battuta was born.
story: Tariq ibn Ziyad sailed from this coast to Spain in 711. Ibn Battuta was born here in 1304 and left at 21 for Hajj, beginning nearly thirty years of travel across the Muslim world and beyond.

name: Timbuktu
line: A desert-edge city of mosques and manuscripts on the bend of the Niger.
story: After his famous Hajj of 1324, Mansa Musa had the Djinguereber mosque built here. Under Mali and Songhai, Timbuktu's mosques, above all Sankore, were centres of learning, and families still keep thousands of manuscripts. Its great scholar Ahmad Baba was taken to Morocco after 1591.

name: Gao
line: Capital of the Songhai empire on the Niger, where Askia Muhammad's tomb stands.
story: Gao's kings embraced Islam around 1000. Askia Muhammad, who made the Hajj in 1496-1497, ruled the Songhai empire from here, and his pyramid-shaped mud-brick tomb still stands. A Moroccan army ended Songhai power at nearby Tondibi in 1591.

name: Tondibi
line: The Niger riverbank where Moroccan guns broke the Songhai empire in 1591.
story: An army sent across the Sahara by the Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, armed with muskets and cannon, defeated the far larger Songhai army of Askia Ishaq II here. Songhai broke apart, and the great age of West African empires ended.

name: Djenne
line: A river town in Mali with the largest mud-brick building in the world.
story: An old centre of trade and Islamic learning in the inland Niger delta. Its Great Mosque, rebuilt in 1907 on the site of earlier mosques, is the largest mud-brick building on earth, and the townspeople replaster it together every year.

name: Sokoto
line: Capital of the Sokoto Caliphate founded by the scholar Usman dan Fodio.
story: From 1804 the scholar Usman dan Fodio led a reform movement that united much of today's northern Nigeria; Sokoto, founded in 1809, became its capital. Its scholars wrote hundreds of works in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa, among them those of his daughter Nana Asma'u.

name: Dakar
line: Capital of Senegal, a mostly Muslim nation shaped by its Sufi orders.
story: Senegal won independence from France in 1960 with Dakar as its capital. Its Islam is shaped by Sufi orders such as the Muridiyya of Amadou Bamba, whose holy city of Touba lies inland.

name: Kilwa
line: An island city-state of the Swahili coast that grew rich on the gold trade.
story: Kilwa Kisiwani controlled the trade in gold from the Zimbabwe plateau. Its Great Mosque dates in part from the 11th century. Ibn Battuta visited in 1331 and called it one of the most beautiful cities, and the Portuguese sacked it in 1505.

name: Zanzibar
line: An island off East Africa with one of the coast's oldest mosques and a sultan from Oman.
story: The mosque at Kizimkazi carries an inscription dated 1107. The sultan of Oman, Sayyid Sa'id, moved his capital here in 1840, and Stone Town grew rich on cloves and, darkly, on the slave trade. A British bombardment in 1896 is called the shortest war in history.

name: Mogadishu
line: One of the oldest Muslim trading towns of East Africa.
story: A Muslim port by the 900s, it grew rich trading with Arabia, Persia and India. Ibn Battuta stayed in 1331 and described its sultan, scholars and fine cloth. Zheng He's Chinese fleets called here in the 1410s.

name: Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq)
line: The rock named after Tariq ibn Ziyad, who landed here in 711 and opened Spain.
story: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Africa in 711 with a Berber and Arab army and landed by this rock. Within a few years most of Spain was Muslim. The Arabic Jabal Tariq, 'Tariq's mountain', became the name Gibraltar.

name: Cordoba
line: Capital of al-Andalus, once among the largest and most learned cities in Europe.
story: Abd al-Rahman I, the Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasids, made it his capital in 756 and began its Great Mosque. Under the caliphate of Abd al-Rahman III in the 900s it had paved streets, lamps and great libraries. Ibn Hazm and Ibn Rushd were born here; Castile took the city in 1236.

name: Toledo
line: The old Visigothic capital, whose fall in 1085 opened a translation bridge from Arabic to Latin.
story: Tariq ibn Ziyad took Toledo in 711. Its fall to Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085 shocked al-Andalus and brought the Almoravids over from Morocco. Under Christian rule, translators in Toledo turned Arabic works of al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd into Latin for Europe.

name: Seville
line: A river port of al-Andalus whose Almohad minaret survives as the Giralda.
story: Musa ibn Nusayr took Seville in 712. It flourished as a taifa kingdom under the poet-king al-Mu'tamid and then as the Almohad capital in Spain, when its great mosque was built. Castile took it in 1248; the minaret survives as the cathedral's Giralda.

name: Granada
line: The last Muslim kingdom of Spain, crowned by the Alhambra, which fell in 1492.
story: The Nasrids ruled Granada from 1238 to 1492 and built the Alhambra palace, its walls covered with the motto 'There is no victor but Allah'. On 2 January 1492 Muhammad XII handed its keys to Ferdinand and Isabella. Within a century the Muslims of Spain were forcibly converted, then expelled (1609-1614).

name: Las Navas de Tolosa
line: The 1212 battle Arab writers called al-Iqab, which broke Almohad power in Spain.
story: The Christian kings of Spain, united under a crusade, defeated the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir here in 1212. Within forty years Cordoba and Seville had fallen, and only Granada remained Muslim.

name: Tours and Poitiers
line: The 732 battle in France that Arab historians called 'the Pavement of the Martyrs'.
story: In 732, somewhere between Poitiers and Tours, Charles Martel's Franks stopped a raid from al-Andalus and killed its leader, the governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi. It marked the northern limit of Muslim armies in western Europe.
note: The exact battlefield is unknown; the pin is at Tours.

name: Aachen
line: Charlemagne's capital, which received an elephant from Harun al-Rashid.
story: Harun al-Rashid exchanged embassies with Charlemagne. His gifts included an elephant named Abul-Abbas, which reached Aachen in 802, and later a water clock that astonished the Franks.

name: Palermo
line: Capital of Muslim Sicily, where al-Idrisi drew his world map for a Norman king.
story: The Aghlabids took Palermo in 831 and it became the capital of Muslim Sicily, with hundreds of mosques. After the Normans conquered the island, King Roger II kept Arabic culture at court, and in 1154 al-Idrisi finished his great world geography for him here.

name: Larnaca (Cyprus)
line: Where Umm Haram, the woman who dreamed of sailing for Allah, is buried.
story: The Prophet ﷺ once woke smiling and told Umm Haram of believers riding the sea like kings on thrones; she asked to be among them. Years later, in Mu'awiyah's sea campaign to Cyprus around 649, she fell from her mount and died. Her tomb, the Hala Sultan Tekke, stands by the salt lake.

name: Rome
line: Capital of the empire that ruled Palestine in Isa's time.
story: Roman governors ruled Palestine when Isa preached, and Rome destroyed Jerusalem's Temple in 70 CE. The empire later became Christian, and its eastern half, al-Rum, is named in the Quran (30:2). Rome itself was sacked in 410, and the western empire ended in 476.
note: A hadith in Ahmad says Constantinople will be conquered before Rome; its grading is discussed.

name: Vienna
line: The Habsburg capital where Ottoman expansion into Europe was twice turned back.
story: Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna in 1529 and withdrew before winter. In 1683 Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa tried again, but a relief army under the Polish king Jan Sobieski broke the siege. A long Ottoman retreat from central Europe followed.

name: Sarajevo
line: An Ottoman-founded city, heart of one of Europe's oldest native Muslim peoples.
story: Founded as an Ottoman town in the 1460s, it grew around the Gazi Husrev Beg Mosque of 1531. It became the heart of Bosnian Islam. The murder of an Austrian archduke here in 1914 set off the First World War, which ended the Ottoman empire.

name: Lepanto
line: The 1571 sea battle where a Holy League fleet destroyed the Ottoman navy.
story: Off Lepanto (Nafpaktos) in western Greece, a fleet of Spain, Venice and the Pope destroyed the Ottoman navy in 1571. The Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year and kept Cyprus, but their unchallenged rule of the Mediterranean was over.

name: Caffa (Crimea)
line: A Crimean port from which the Black Death is said to have sailed to Europe.
story: The Golden Horde besieged this Genoese port in 1346. Plague broke out in the camp and passed to the city, and Genoese ships carried it to the Mediterranean. The Black Death killed perhaps a third of Europe and the Middle East, Cairo and Damascus included.
note: The story of corpses thrown over the walls comes from a single Italian chronicler.

name: Kazan
line: Tatar city on the Volga, heir to the Bulgars who accepted Islam in 922.
story: The Volga Bulgars accepted Islam in 922, when the caliph's envoy Ibn Fadlan visited them. Kazan became the seat of a khanate after the Golden Horde split, until Ivan the Terrible conquered it in 1552. Its Tatars remain one of Europe's oldest Muslim peoples.
note: Ibn Fadlan visited the Bulgar capital near later Kazan, not Kazan itself.

name: Paris
line: Capital of France, whose Revolution of 1789 sent new ideas and armies into the Muslim world.
story: The French Revolution spread ideas of nation and secular rule that reshaped Muslim lands, beginning with Napoleon's invasion of Egypt in 1798. Its Grand Mosque opened in 1926 to honour Muslim soldiers who died for France in the First World War.

name: Wittenberg
line: The German town where the Protestant Reformation began in 1517.
story: Martin Luther posted his ninety-five theses here in 1517. Many historians argue that Ottoman pressure on the Habsburgs in the same decades helped Protestantism survive.

name: Mount Judi
line: The mountain where Nuh's ark came to rest after the Flood.
story: 'And the ship came to rest on al-Judi' (11:44). Muslim tradition identifies it with Cudi Dagh near Cizre in southeast Turkey, above the Tigris, and the Muslim geographers wrote of a shrine to Nuh nearby.
note: Some place Judi elsewhere; the Bible names 'the mountains of Ararat'.

name: Mohenjo-daro
line: A planned brick city of the Indus valley, abandoned around 1900 BCE.
story: With straight streets, drains and a great bath, Mohenjo-daro flourished around 2500 BCE and was later abandoned. Its people and script remain a mystery, one of the many nations before us whose story only Allah knows in full.

name: Anyang
line: Last capital of China's Shang kings, where the earliest Chinese writing was found.
story: From about 1300 to 1046 BCE the Shang kings ruled from here and asked questions of their ancestors on oracle bones, the oldest Chinese writing. The Quran says a messenger was sent to every nation (16:36), though it names only a few.

name: Bodh Gaya
line: The place in India linked to the Buddha, around 500 BCE.
story: Buddhists hold that the Buddha reached enlightenment under a tree here. The Quran says among the messengers are 'those whose stories We have not related to you' (40:78), so Muslims neither affirm nor deny unnamed figures.

name: Gaugamela
line: The plain near Mosul where Alexander ended the Persian empire in 331 BCE.
story: Alexander the Great defeated Darius III here and took the Persian empire. Some Muslim writers identified Alexander with Dhul-Qarnayn; many scholars, Ibn Kathir among them, rejected this, since Alexander was an idol-worshipper.

name: Cave of the Sleepers
line: The cave where young believers and their dog slept for 309 years.
story: Young believers fled a ruler who forced idol worship and slept in a cave for 309 years (18:25), their dog stretched at the entrance. The Quran leaves the place unnamed and warns against arguing over details. Christian tradition placed it at Ephesus in Turkey; Muslim traditions also point to a cave near Amman, called al-Raqim, and to Tarsus.
note: All sites are traditional; the pin is at Ephesus. 'Al-Raqim' may be an inscribed tablet rather than a place.

name: Mongolia (Karakorum)
line: Steppe homeland of Genghis Khan, whose grandsons destroyed Baghdad and then embraced Islam.
story: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206, and his heirs ruled from Karakorum the largest land empire in history. Within a century, the Mongol khans of Persia, the Golden Horde and Central Asia had become Muslims.

name: Istanbul (Constantinople)
line: The city of Constantine, besieged by the early Muslims and taken by Mehmed II in 1453.
story: Constantine made it the new Rome in 330, and for a thousand years it was the Christian capital of the east. Muslim armies besieged it in the 670s and 717; Abu Ayyub al-Ansari died during an early siege and is buried by its walls. Mehmed II took it in 1453, and it became the Ottoman capital.
note: The hadith in Ahmad, 'Constantinople will be conquered; excellent is its commander', is graded weak by many scholars. 30:2-4 refers to the Byzantines (al-Rum), whose capital this was.

name: Bursa
line: The first great Ottoman capital, where the early sultans are buried.
story: Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it the Ottoman capital. Bayezid I built its twenty-domed Grand Mosque around 1400 after his victory at Nicopolis. Osman and Orhan are buried here, and its silk trade made it rich.

name: Sogut
line: A small Anatolian town where the Ottoman state was born around 1299.
story: Ertugrul's Turkish clan settled here on the Byzantine frontier, and his son Osman began the Ottoman state around 1299. Ertugrul's tomb is in the town.

name: Konya
line: Capital of the Seljuks of Rum and resting place of Jalal al-Din Rumi.
story: Ancient Iconium became capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum after 1097. Jalal al-Din Rumi settled here as a refugee from the Mongol advance and wrote his Masnavi; his green-domed tomb still draws visitors. Its Seljuk mosques and colleges are among the finest in Anatolia.

name: Ankara
line: Site of Timur's crushing of the Ottomans in 1402 and capital of the Turkish Republic.
story: Near here in 1402 Timur defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, nearly ending the young empire. Five centuries later Ankara became the capital of the Turkish Republic, which abolished the Ottoman caliphate in 1924.

name: Manzikert
line: The 1071 battle that opened Anatolia to the Turks.
story: In August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV here, then treated him with honour and freed him. Turkish settlers poured into Anatolia, the first step toward today's Turkey, and an alarmed Byzantium asked the West for help, which fed the Crusades.

name: Yarmuk
line: The river gorge where the Muslims defeated the Byzantine army in 636.
story: In August 636, where today's Jordan, Syria and the Golan meet, a Muslim army led by Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a much larger Byzantine force over six days. Heraclius left Syria for good.
note: Heraclius's reported words of farewell to Syria come from later Arab historians.

name: Hattin
line: The twin-peaked hill above Galilee where Salah al-Din destroyed the Crusader army in 1187.
story: On 4 July 1187 Salah al-Din trapped a thirsty Crusader army here and destroyed it, capturing King Guy and executing Reynald of Chatillon, who had attacked pilgrims and threatened Madinah. Three months later Jerusalem was his. A shrine nearby is held by local tradition to be the tomb of Shuayb.
note: The tomb of Shuayb at Hattin is a local tradition (Druze and Muslim); other sites are also claimed.

name: Acre
line: The port that was the last great Crusader stronghold, retaken by the Mamluks in 1291.
story: Salah al-Din took Acre in 1187, lost it to Richard I after a long siege in 1191, and it became the Crusader capital. The Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil captured it in 1291, ending the Crusader states. In 1799 its walls turned back Napoleon.

name: Gaza
line: An old trading town where the Prophet's ﷺ great-grandfather Hashim is buried and al-Shafi'i was born.
story: Quraysh's summer caravans ran to Gaza and Syria (106:2). Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, who began those caravans, died and was buried here; the town is still called Ghazzat Hashim. Imam al-Shafi'i was born in Gaza in 767.
note: Hashim's founding of the two caravans and burial at Gaza are from the Sirah and early histories.

name: Ain Jalut
line: 'Goliath's Spring', where the Mamluks stopped the Mongols in 1260.
story: In the Jezreel Valley, at a spring named after Jalut, the Mamluks under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army on 3 September 1260, two years after Baghdad fell. It was the first decisive Mongol defeat in the region and saved Egypt and the holy cities.
note: The name's link to Jalut is popular tradition.

name: Nahavand
line: The 'Victory of Victories', which broke Sasanian Persia in 642.
story: In the Zagros mountains in 642, the Muslims defeated the last great Sasanian field army; Muslims called it 'the Victory of Victories'. Its commander, al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin, was martyred. Yazdegerd III fled east, and the Persian empire never recovered.

name: Hamadan
line: Ancient Ecbatana, where Ibn Sina served as vizier and is buried.
story: Hamadan was Ecbatana, capital of the Medes. Ibn Sina served as vizier to its ruler and died here in 1037; his tomb is the city's landmark.

name: Isfahan
line: 'Half the world': Seljuk capital and the jewel of Safavid Persia.
story: Taken by the Muslims in the 640s, it was a Seljuk capital, and its Friday Mosque holds work from many dynasties. Ibn Sina worked here for years. Shah Abbas I made it the Safavid capital in 1598 and built the vast Naqsh-e Jahan square; Persians said 'Isfahan is half the world'.

name: Shiraz
line: City of poets in southern Persia, resting place of Sa'di and Hafiz.
story: Shiraz grew as a Muslim city from the 690s and became the cultural capital of southern Persia. The poets Sa'di and Hafiz are buried here, and Sibawayh, father of Arabic grammar, came from this region.

name: Tabriz
line: Ilkhanid capital and birthplace of the Safavid state in 1501.
story: The Mongol Ilkhans ruled from Tabriz, where the vizier Rashid al-Din wrote a history of the world. Shams of Tabriz, Rumi's companion, came from here. Ismail I was crowned here in 1501, founding the Safavid state that made Twelver Shi'ism Iran's official faith.

name: Tehran (and Rayy)
line: Iran's capital, beside the ruins of Rayy, city of the two al-Razis.
story: Ancient Rayy, just south, was a great Abbasid city and home of the physician Abu Bakr al-Razi and the theologian Fakhr al-Din al-Razi; the Mongols ruined it. Tehran became the Qajar capital in 1796 and the capital of modern Iran.

name: Tus
line: The town of al-Ghazali, Firdawsi and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, where Harun al-Rashid died.
story: Near today's Mashhad, Tus was the birthplace of al-Ghazali, the poet Firdawsi and the scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. The caliph Harun al-Rashid died here on campaign in 809.

name: Nishapur
line: A great city of Khurasan, home of Imam Muslim and Omar Khayyam.
story: Nishapur was home of the hadith master Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, the poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam and the Sufi poet Farid al-Din Attar. Its Nizamiyya college was famous, and al-Ghazali studied there under al-Juwayni. The Mongols massacred its people in 1221.

name: Merv
line: The oasis where the last Sasanian king died and the Abbasid revolution began.
story: The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651. Abu Muslim raised the black banners of the Abbasid revolution here in 747, and it later became the Seljuk capital under Sultan Sanjar. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221.

name: Herat
line: An oasis city that reached its golden age under the Timurids in the 1400s.
story: Herat joined the Muslim world in the 650s. Rebuilt after the Mongols, it flourished under the Timurids, when Shah Rukh and his wife Gawhar Shad endowed mosques and colleges, and the painter Bihzad and the poet Jami worked here.

name: Bukhara
line: Silk Road city of the Samanids, which gave the world Imam al-Bukhari and Ibn Sina.
story: Qutayba ibn Muslim took Bukhara around 709. Under the Samanids it was a capital of Persian and Islamic learning, birthplace of Imam al-Bukhari, and Ibn Sina studied in its royal library. Genghis Khan burned it in 1220.

name: Samarkand
line: Timur's blue-domed capital, where Ulugh Beg mapped the stars.
story: Qutayba ibn Muslim took Samarkand in 712, and tradition holds that the Prophet's ﷺ cousin Qutham ibn Abbas is buried at its Shah-i Zinda. Timur made it his capital, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory that charted over a thousand stars.
note: Paper-making is said to have come here from Chinese prisoners after Talas (751); the story is debated.

name: Khwarazm (Urgench)
line: The delta land of the Oxus that gave its name to al-Khwarizmi and to the algorithm.
story: The mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us 'algorithm', came from this land, and al-Biruni was born here. Its shahs ruled a great empire until Genghis Khan destroyed their capital Gurganj, today's Kunya-Urgench, in 1221.

name: Talas
line: The river where Abbasid and Tang armies met in 751, the only battle between caliphate and China.
story: By the Talas river in 751 an Abbasid army defeated Tang China. Central Asia stayed in the Muslim world, and Tang China soon turned inward after a great rebellion.
note: The story that captured Chinese papermakers then taught their craft in Samarkand is old but debated.

name: Tashkent
line: The oasis the Arabs called al-Shash, home of an early Quran linked to Uthman.
story: Al-Shash joined the Muslim world in the 700s. Russia conquered it in 1865 and made it the capital of Turkestan. An early Quran manuscript, traditionally linked to the caliph Uthman and once kept in Samarkand, is now kept here.
note: Scholars date the Tashkent Quran to the 8th or 9th century; its link to Uthman is traditional.

name: Debal
line: The old port of Sindh where Muhammad ibn al-Qasim landed in 711.
story: Pirates sailing from Debal seized ships carrying Muslim women and pilgrims from Sri Lanka. In 711 the young general Muhammad ibn al-Qasim stormed the port and went on to take Sindh and Multan. Islam took root in the Indus valley from here.
note: The ruins at Banbhore, east of Karachi, are the likely site.

name: Multan
line: The 'city of saints' in Punjab, taken by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim in 713.
story: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim took Multan in 713. It became an outpost of Islam in India for centuries, and later a city of Sufi shrines, among them that of Shah Rukn-e-Alam.

name: Karachi
line: Pakistan's first capital and great port.
story: A fishing village that grew into a great port under British rule. It became Pakistan's first capital in 1947; Muhammad Ali Jinnah was born and is buried here.

name: Ghazni
line: Capital of Mahmud of Ghazni, patron of Firdawsi and al-Biruni.
story: Mahmud of Ghazni (998-1030) raided deep into India and gathered poets and scholars to his court. Firdawsi presented the Shahnameh to him, and al-Biruni travelled with his armies to write his great book on India. Two brick minarets of his successors still stand.

name: Kabul
line: Mountain city on the road to India, Babur's first capital and resting place.
story: Babur took Kabul in 1504 and ruled from here before founding the Mughal empire in India. By his wish he is buried in its Bagh-e Babur garden.

name: Lahore
line: Punjab's city of saints and Mughal gardens, resting place of Ali Hujwiri and Iqbal.
story: Lahore came under the Ghaznavids in the 11th century. The Sufi Ali Hujwiri, author of Kashf al-Mahjub, is buried here at Data Darbar. The Mughals made it a capital of gardens; Aurangzeb's Badshahi Mosque (1673) is among the largest in the world, and the poet Muhammad Iqbal lies at its gate.

name: Delhi
line: Capital of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, a city of saints and scholars.
story: Delhi became the sultanate's capital in 1206; the Qutb Minar was begun around 1199. Nizam al-Din Awliya taught here, and Shah Wali Allah renewed hadith study in the 1700s. Shah Jahan built the Red Fort and Jama Masjid, and after 1857 the British exiled the last Mughal emperor.

name: Agra
line: Mughal capital on the Yamuna, home of the Taj Mahal.
story: Akbar ruled from Agra's Red Fort and nearby Fatehpur Sikri. His grandson Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal (1632-1653) as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, its marble inscribed with Quranic verses on Judgement and Paradise.

name: Panipat
line: The plain north of Delhi where three battles decided the fate of India.
story: Babur defeated the Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi here in 1526 and founded the Mughal empire. Akbar's army won here in 1556, and Ahmad Shah Durrani defeated the Marathas here in 1761.

name: Plassey
line: The 1757 battle that began British rule in India.
story: The East India Company under Robert Clive defeated Siraj al-Dawla, Nawab of Bengal, here in 1757, helped by the betrayal of his commander Mir Jafar. Within a century Britain ruled most of India.

name: Calicut
line: A spice port on India's Malabar coast where Vasco da Gama landed in 1498.
story: Arab and Indian Muslim merchants had traded at Calicut for centuries. Vasco da Gama's arrival in 1498 began a Portuguese sea war on Muslim shipping, recorded by the local scholar Zayn al-Din al-Ma'bari in his Tuhfat al-Mujahidin.

name: Samudra Pasai
line: A Sumatran port, the first known Muslim kingdom of Southeast Asia.
story: The gravestone of its first sultan, Malik al-Salih, is dated 1297. Ibn Battuta visited in 1345 and found a sultan who loved to debate fiqh with scholars. The name Sumatra comes from Samudra.

name: Malacca
line: The port on the great strait from which Islam spread through the Malay world.
story: Its ruler embraced Islam in the early 1400s, and Malacca became the hub from which Islam spread across the Malay world by trade and marriage. Zheng He's fleets called here. The Portuguese seized it in 1511, and Muslim trade moved to Aceh, Johor and Brunei.

name: Aceh
line: The 'Veranda of Makkah', where Southeast Asian pilgrims set sail for Hajj.
story: At the northern tip of Sumatra, Aceh was the last port before the Indian Ocean crossing to Arabia. Its sultanate peaked under Iskandar Muda (1607-1636), sought Ottoman help against the Portuguese, and fought the Dutch for decades from 1873.

name: Xi'an (Chang'an)
line: Tang China's capital at the eastern end of the Silk Road, home of an ancient mosque.
story: Chang'an was the largest city of its age. A Muslim embassy reached the Tang court in 651, in Uthman's caliphate, and Arab and Persian merchants settled here. Its Great Mosque, built like a Chinese temple, is one of China's oldest.
note: The 651 embassy is recorded in the Tang histories. The mosque's founding date (traditionally 742) is uncertain; most of the present buildings are Ming.

name: Guangzhou (Canton)
line: The southern Chinese port Arab sailors called Khanfu, with one of China's oldest mosques.
story: From the 700s a large community of Muslim traders lived here. Its Huaisheng mosque, with a lighthouse-like minaret, is among the oldest in China, and Chinese Muslim tradition links it and a nearby tomb to the Companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.
note: That Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas travelled to China is a Chinese Muslim tradition; the Arabic sources say he died near Madinah and was buried in al-Baqi.

name: Quanzhou (Zaytun)
line: The great medieval port Arab sailors called Zaytun.
story: Muslim merchants made Quanzhou their home; its Qingjing mosque dates from 1009. Tradition says two Companions of the Prophet ﷺ are buried on Lingshan hill. Ibn Battuta landed here in 1345 and called its harbour one of the greatest in the world.
note: The tradition about the two Companions' tombs is not established.

name: Nanjing
line: Early Ming capital, from which the Muslim admiral Zheng He sailed.
story: From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He, a Muslim from Yunnan, led seven great fleets from here across the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa. Some of his men made the pilgrimage to Makkah.

name: Diriyah
line: The mud-brick town where the first Saudi state was born in 1744.
story: In 1744 the preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the local ruler Muhammad ibn Saud made a pact here that founded the first Saudi state. An Ottoman-Egyptian army destroyed it in 1818.

name: Riyadh
line: The Najd oasis from which the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was built.
story: In 1902 the young Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud retook Riyadh, his family's old seat, in a night raid. From here he united most of Arabia, including the Hijaz with Makkah and Madinah, and proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.

name: Dammam
line: The Gulf coast town where oil was found in 1938.
story: In 1938 the well known as Dammam Number 7 struck oil in commercial quantity. The wealth that followed transformed Arabia and, in time, the scale of the Hajj and the holy mosques.

name: Arabia
line: The peninsula of deserts, oases and trade roads where the final Messenger ﷺ was sent.
story: Before Islam, Arabia was a land of tribes, poets and caravan towns, between the empires of Rome and Persia. Hud, Salih and Shuayb were sent to its ancient peoples, and Ibrahim and Ismail built the Kaaba in its heart. Within the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime it was united under Islam for the first time.

name: Palestine
line: The heart of the Holy Land, between the Jordan and the sea.
story: Many prophets lived and preached here, from Ibrahim to Isa, and its centre is Jerusalem. The Muslims took it from Byzantium in the 630s. It was fought over in the Crusades, ruled by the Mamluks and Ottomans, and after 1917 by Britain.

name: The Euphrates
line: The great river of Iraq, which the Prophet ﷺ said will one day uncover a mountain of gold.
story: Ur, Babylon, Kufa and Karbala all grew on the Euphrates and its channels, and Mari and Raqqa on its upper course. Among the signs of the Hour, the Prophet ﷺ said it will uncover a treasure of gold, and warned believers not to take from it.

name: Nubia
line: The Nile land south of Egypt, linked by some commentators to Luqman.
story: Nubia's kingdoms traded and fought with Egypt for thousands of years and later became Christian. Some commentators said the wise man Luqman was a Nubian. In 652 the Muslims of Egypt and the Nubian kingdom of Makuria signed the Baqt treaty, which kept peace for six centuries.
note: That Luqman was Nubian is one view of the commentators; others say Ethiopian or Egyptian.

name: Punjab
line: The 'land of five rivers', gateway of Islam into northern India.
story: Muslim armies reached it from Sindh in 713 and from Ghazni after 1000. Lahore became its great Muslim city, and its Sufi saints, among them Baba Farid, drew many people to Islam.

name: al-Abwa
line: The village between Makkah and Madinah where the Prophet's ﷺ mother Aminah died.
story: Aminah took her six-year-old son to Yathrib to visit his relatives; on the way back she fell ill and died at al-Abwa. Years later, the Prophet ﷺ visited her grave and wept. His first expedition after the Hijrah, in 623, came here.

name: Ukaz
line: The great fair of pre-Islamic Arabia, where poets competed and the Prophet ﷺ called the tribes.
story: Each year Arabs gathered at Ukaz near Ta'if to trade, settle disputes and recite poetry; the prized odes were later called the Mu'allaqat. The Prophet ﷺ went among the tribes here calling them to Allah. The jinn heard the Quran on one such journey toward the market.

name: al-Muraysi'
line: The well near the Red Sea coast where the Banu al-Mustaliq were defeated in 627.
story: On the return from this campaign Aishah was left behind looking for a lost necklace, and hypocrites spread a slander about her. Allah declared her innocence in Surah al-Nur (24:11-20). Juwayriyah, daughter of the tribe's chief, married the Prophet ﷺ, and her people were freed.
note: Some date the campaign to 626. Coordinates are approximate.

name: Bi'r Ma'unah
line: The well in Najd where about seventy Quran reciters were treacherously killed in 625.
story: The Prophet ﷺ sent about seventy Companions known for their Quran to teach a Najdi tribe at its request. At this well they were ambushed and killed. Grieved, the Prophet ﷺ supplicated against the killers in the Qunut of the prayer for a month.
note: The story and the month of Qunut are reported by Bukhari and Muslim. Coordinates are approximate.

name: al-Yamamah
line: The Najd region where Musaylimah's rebellion was crushed in 632, at a great cost of reciters.
story: Musaylimah claimed prophethood here and gathered a large army. In 632 Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated him at Aqraba, in the 'garden of death'. So many Quran memorisers fell that Umar urged Abu Bakr to collect the Quran into one book.

name: Amwas (Emmaus)
line: The village whose plague in 639 took Abu Ubaydah, Mu'adh and thousands of the Companions' army.
story: The plague of Amwas struck Syria in 638-639 and killed perhaps 25,000 Muslims. Umar turned back from visiting Syria, following the Prophet's ﷺ teaching not to enter a land of plague. Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah and Mu'adh ibn Jabal died as martyrs.

name: Lod (Ludd)
line: The town at whose gate, the Prophet ﷺ said, Isa will kill the Dajjal.
story: Lydda was an old town of Palestine and later a Muslim provincial centre. In the long hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, the Prophet ﷺ said Isa will pursue the Dajjal and catch him at the gate of Ludd, and kill him there.

name: Machaerus
line: Herod's hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, where Yahya is said to have been killed.
story: The historian Josephus wrote that Herod Antipas imprisoned and executed Yahya (John the Baptist) at this fortress in Jordan. The Quran praises Yahya as 'honorable, abstaining from women, and a prophet' (3:39) and sends peace on him the day he died (19:15).
note: Muslim reports differ on where Yahya was killed; some say Damascus, where a shrine to him stands in the Umayyad Mosque.

name: Siffin
line: The Euphrates plain where Ali and Mu'awiyah's armies met in 657 and agreed to arbitration.
story: In 657 the armies of Ali and Mu'awiyah faced each other here for weeks. When Qurans were raised on spears, the fighting stopped and both sides agreed to arbitration. Muslims hold that Companions on both sides acted by their own judgement, and they pray for them all.

name: Nahrawan
line: The canal east of Baghdad where Ali defeated the Khawarij in 658.
story: A group who rejected the arbitration after Siffin declared other Muslims unbelievers and took up arms. Ali defeated them here in 658. The Prophet ﷺ had described such people, who recite the Quran without it passing their throats.
note: The hadith about the Khawarij is reported by Bukhari and Muslim.

name: al-Namara
line: The desert site of a 328 CE tomb inscription, one of the oldest texts in the Arabic language.
