story: The Namara inscription marks the tomb of Imru' al-Qays ibn Amr, called 'king of all the Arabs'. Written in Nabataean letters, its language is early Arabic, three centuries before the Quran came down 'in a clear Arabic language' (26:195).

name: Zafar
line: The mountain capital of Himyar, last great kingdom of pre-Islamic Yemen.
story: Zafar was the seat of the Himyarite kings, who ruled Yemen from about 110 BCE to the 520s. Its kings turned to Judaism, and the last of them, Dhu Nuwas, persecuted the Christians of Najran before Aksum overthrew him.

name: The Valley of the Ants
line: The valley where an ant warned her colony of Sulayman's army, and he smiled.
story: As Sulayman's army of men, jinn and birds came upon a valley, an ant said: 'O ants, enter your dwellings that you not be crushed by Solomon and his soldiers while they perceive not' (27:18). He smiled and thanked Allah for His favour. The valley's place is unknown.
note: Commentators name different places, in Syria, Ta'if and elsewhere; the pin is a placeholder in Palestine.

name: Thebes (Luxor)
line: Capital of Egypt's New Kingdom, the age most historians link to Musa's Firaun.
story: Thebes, today's Luxor, held the great temples of Karnak and the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings. Many historians place the Exodus in the New Kingdom, often under Ramesses II, though no one knows. The Quran keeps the tyrant's name hidden and calls him only Firaun.
note: Which pharaoh faced Musa is unknown; Ramesses II and Merneptah are only the most popular guesses.

name: Pi-Ramesses (Avaris)
line: The delta capital of Ramesses II, where many place Bani Israil's slavery.
story: Built by Ramesses II on the site of older Avaris, where Semitic settlers from Canaan had once lived and even ruled. Many historians link the area to Bani Israil's time in Egypt, from Yusuf's family to Musa.
note: The link with Bani Israil is a historian's theory, not established.

name: Persepolis
line: Ceremonial capital of the Persian kings, burned by Alexander in 330 BCE.
story: Darius I began the palace terraces around 518 BCE, where peoples of the empire brought tribute. Alexander burned it in 330 BCE. Persia's Cyrus, who freed Bani Israil from Babylon, is held by some modern scholars to be Dhul-Qarnayn.
note: The Cyrus view of Dhul-Qarnayn is one opinion among several.

name: Nicaea (Iznik)
line: Where the church council of 325 defined the Trinity, and later the first Seljuk capital in Anatolia.
story: In 325 Constantine gathered bishops here to settle Isa's nature, and the creed they made declared him God. The Quran answers: 'The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah... do not say Three' (4:171). The Seljuks took Nicaea in 1081, and its later tiles adorned Ottoman mosques.

name: Balkh
line: 'Mother of Cities' in Khurasan, birthplace of Rumi and home of Ibrahim ibn Adham.
story: One of the oldest cities of Central Asia, Balkh entered Islam in the 650s and became a great centre of learning. The prince Ibrahim ibn Adham left its throne for a life of worship, and Rumi was born here around 1207 before his family fled the Mongols, who ruined the city in 1220.

name: Otrar
line: The Silk Road town whose massacre of a Mongol caravan in 1218 brought Genghis Khan west.
story: Otrar's governor killed a Mongol trade caravan, and the Khwarazm Shah then killed Genghis Khan's envoy. The Mongol storm that followed destroyed the cities of Central Asia and Persia. The philosopher al-Farabi was born in the Otrar district.

name: Sarai
line: Capital of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga, whose khans embraced Islam.
story: Batu Khan founded Sarai around 1250. His brother Berke became the first Mongol khan to accept Islam and allied with the Mamluks against his cousin Hulagu. Under Uzbek Khan in the 1300s, the Horde became Muslim.

name: al-Mansurah
line: The Nile delta town where the Crusade of Louis IX was crushed in 1250.
story: In 1250 the Mamluk guard, led by Baybars, trapped Louis IX's crusaders in the streets of Mansurah, and the French king was soon captured. Shajar al-Durr held the state together after her husband's death, and within months the Mamluks took power.

name: Chaldiran
line: The 1514 battle where Ottoman guns defeated the Safavids and fixed the border of Turkey and Iran.
story: Sultan Selim I defeated Shah Ismail I here with artillery and muskets. Selim then turned south and took Syria, Egypt and the protection of Makkah and Madinah in 1516-1517.

name: Gallipoli
line: The straits where the Ottomans held back the Allied invasion of 1915.
story: In 1915 Britain and France tried to force the Dardanelles and take Istanbul. Ottoman troops held the peninsula through months of slaughter, and Mustafa Kemal made his name here. The empire survived the battle but not the war.

name: Khartoum
line: City of the two Niles, taken by the Sudanese Mahdi's army in 1885.
story: Founded by Egypt in the 1820s where the White and Blue Nile meet. Muhammad Ahmad, who claimed to be the Mahdi, took it in 1885 and killed the British general Gordon. Britain retook Sudan in 1898.
note: Mainstream scholars rejected Muhammad Ahmad's claim to be the Mahdi.

name: Deoband
line: Town of the Darul Uloom, founded in 1866 to keep Islamic learning alive under British rule.
story: After the failed revolt of 1857, scholars led by Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi founded the Darul Uloom here in 1866. It became one of the most influential madrasas in the world, with thousands of daughter schools across South Asia and beyond.

name: Aligarh
line: Home of the college Sayyid Ahmad Khan founded in 1875 to join modern learning with faith.
story: Sayyid Ahmad Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College here in 1875, which became Aligarh Muslim University. Its graduates shaped Muslim politics in British India.

name: Koumbi Saleh
line: Probable capital of ancient Ghana, with a Muslim town of twelve mosques.
story: The Andalusi geographer al-Bakri wrote in 1068 that Ghana's capital had two towns: the king's town and a Muslim merchants' town with twelve mosques, imams and scholars. The ruins of Koumbi Saleh in Mauritania are thought to be that city.
note: The identification with al-Bakri's Ghana capital is likely, not certain.

name: Niani
line: Traditional capital of the Mali empire of Sundiata and Mansa Musa.
story: Oral tradition makes Niani the capital of Sundiata Keita, founder of Mali in the 1230s, and of his successors. From Mali, Mansa Musa set out on his famous Hajj of 1324.
note: Historians debate whether Niani was the main capital of Mali.

name: Kanem (Njimi)
line: The kingdom near Lake Chad whose rulers accepted Islam around 1085.
story: Kanem's king Hume became Muslim around 1085, and his son made the Hajj. Later rulers moved west to Bornu, and the Kanem-Bornu empire lasted for centuries, trading across the Sahara with Libya and Egypt.

name: Mazara
line: The Sicilian port where the Aghlabid conquest of Sicily began in 827.
story: The Maliki judge Asad ibn al-Furat, scholar and general, led the Aghlabid fleet ashore here in 827. He died during the siege of Syracuse, but Sicily became Muslim over the following decades.

name: Mascara
line: The town where Emir Abd al-Qadir was proclaimed leader of Algeria's resistance in 1832.
story: The young scholar Abd al-Qadir received the pledge of the tribes near Mascara in 1832 and fought the French for fifteen years. In exile in Damascus he later sheltered thousands of Christians during the riots of 1860.

name: Gunib
line: Mountain village in Dagestan where Imam Shamil surrendered to Russia in 1859.
story: Imam Shamil led the Muslims of the Caucasus against Russia for twenty-five years. Besieged at Gunib, he surrendered in 1859 and was later allowed to go on Hajj; he died in Madinah in 1871 and is buried in al-Baqi.

name: Palembang
line: Capital of Srivijaya, a Sumatran sea kingdom that traded with the caliphate.
story: Srivijaya ruled the Malacca Strait from about 650 to 1100. Arab writers reported a letter from one of its kings to the caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asking for someone to teach him Islam. Palembang later became a Muslim sultanate.
note: The letter to Umar II is reported by later Arab writers; its details are not certain.

name: Jakarta
line: Capital of Indonesia, the country with the most Muslims in the world.
story: The Dutch ruled the islands from here as Batavia from 1619. Indonesia declared independence in 1945, and its Istiqlal Mosque, opened in 1978, is one of the largest in Southeast Asia.

name: al-Zallaqa (Sagrajas)
line: The 1086 battle near Badajoz where the Almoravids saved al-Andalus for another century.
story: After Toledo fell, the taifa kings of al-Andalus called on Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the Almoravid ruler of Morocco. He crossed the strait and crushed Alfonso VI's army at al-Zallaqa in 1086. The Almoravids then took over al-Andalus themselves.

name: Covadonga
line: The mountain valley in Asturias where the Christian reconquest of Spain is said to have begun.
story: Around 722 a small Christian band under Pelayo defeated a Muslim force in these northern mountains and founded the kingdom of Asturias. Andalusi chroniclers dismissed them as a handful of men; seven centuries later their heirs took Granada.
note: The battle's date and size are uncertain; the Christian chronicles enlarged it.

name: Battle of the Masts
line: The 655 sea battle off Lycia where the young Muslim navy defeated Byzantium.
story: Off Phoenix (Finike) in southern Turkey, the fleet of Egypt and Syria under Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh defeated the Byzantine emperor Constans II. The Arabs called it 'the Battle of the Masts' for the forest of masts lashed together. It opened the Mediterranean to Muslim fleets.

name: Valencia
line: A rich garden city of eastern al-Andalus, famous for its irrigation.
story: Under Muslim rule from 714, Valencia's farmers built the canals and water courts that still work today. El Cid took it in 1094, the Almoravids won it back in 1102, and James I of Aragon conquered it in 1238.

name: Srebrenica
line: The Bosnian town where over 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed in July 1995.
story: During the Bosnian war, Srebrenica was declared a UN safe area, yet in July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces overran it and killed more than 8,000 Bosniak Muslims. International courts ruled it a genocide, the worst massacre in Europe since the Second World War.

name: Cox's Bazar
line: The Bangladeshi coast where about a million Rohingya Muslim refugees live in camps.
story: Rohingya Muslims fleeing violence in Myanmar crossed into Bangladesh in waves, above all in 2017. The camps near Cox's Bazar became among the largest refugee settlements in the world.

name: Fayetteville, North Carolina
line: Home of Omar ibn Said, an enslaved West African scholar who wrote his life story in Arabic.
story: Omar ibn Said, a scholar from Futa Toro in Senegal, was enslaved and shipped to the Carolinas in 1807. In 1831 he wrote a short autobiography in Arabic, opening with Surah al-Mulk, one of the few such texts by an enslaved person in America.
